result.reason: The passage presents Rabbi Meir's view from the baraita — permitting bloodletting only where no mum results — which is exactly what the 'R. Meir Position' section describes, not the stricter Rabbi Yehuda position under which it currently sits.

The passage presents the Rabbis permitting bloodletting even where a mum results but prohibiting slaughter on that basis, Rabbi Shimon permitting slaughter on that basis, and Rabbi Yehuda forbidding all bloodletting — this is the baraita content described in heading 4 ('Sages: No Slaughter'), which is where it currently sits and which matches the passage's content precisely.

The passage introduces the comparison between the baraita dispute and the terumah barrel dispute, which matches exactly the 'Comparison Intro' section prose describing Rabbi Eliezer/Chiyya teaching his son the parallel — 'ke-machloket kan kach machloket be-chavit shel terumah'.

The passage contains both Rabbi Yehoshua's statement and Rabban Gamliel's statement as a single unit, and since it includes Rabbi Yehoshua's view as its primary content, it belongs under the 'R. Yehoshua Terumah' heading which discusses both positions together as part of the same dispute.

The passage explicitly draws the correspondence between Rabbi Meir/Rabbi Eliezer, the Rabbis/Rabbi Yehoshua, and Rabbi Yehuda/Rabban Gamliel, which is precisely what the 'Correspondence' section's prose describes.
The passage directly discusses the direct vs. indirect action distinction (beyadayim vs. garma) which is precisely what the prose under heading 0 describes.
The passage specifically articulates the 'shema yavo Eliyahu' reasoning contrasted with the urgency of the bechor case, which is precisely what heading 0's prose describes as the second objection.
Both items continue the same bidirectional symmetry analysis — reversing each position's logic between the bechor and terumah cases — which is precisely what the 'Objections 3-6' prose describes.

Both items present the two 'hakol modim' precedents (leavening after leavening, castrating after castrating) that candidate 4's prose explicitly describes as the scriptural basis being laid out, matching the current placement exactly.

The passage presents both Rabbi Meir's and the Rabbis' positions together as a single unit explaining the disputed case, and its content (introducing the dispute about blemish-upon-blemish and stating both views) best matches heading 0 'R. Meir: Act Focus,' which is where the essay introduces this very dispute and Rabbi Meir's position — the Rabbis' view is mentioned there as context, whereas heading 1 treats only the Rabbis' elaborated reasoning as a standalone section.

All five items deal with the scriptural basis for extending or limiting the blemish prohibition — Rabbi Meir's use of 'tamim yihyeh le-ratzon,' the exclusion of disqualified consecrated animals after redemption, and the rabbanan's derivation from 'kol mum' to cover indirect causation (grama) — which is precisely what the 'Grama Implication' prose describes.

The passage introduces the verse 'terumotai' as the scriptural basis for the terumah dispute, which matches the 'Guarding Source' prose that discusses this exact verse and its role in establishing the shemirah obligation.

The passage presents both Rabbi Eliezer's and Rabbi Yehoshua's positions as a paired unit explaining their respective readings, and the current heading 'R. Eliezer: Dual' with its prose about the plural reading and dual categories of terumah is the best match for this combined textual item that leads with Rabbi Eliezer's interpretation.

Both items present the bevigdo bah contradiction — Rabbi Akiva reading by vocalization versus Rabbi Eliezer reading by spelling — which is precisely the detour described in the 'Different Bases' prose as the gemara's challenge to Rabbi Eliezer being categorized as following yeish em lamikra.

The passage presents both Rabbi Yehoshua's 'lecha' limiting principle and Rabbi Eliezer's 'shema yavo Eliyahu' counter-argument together as a unified dispute, but the 'Benefit Logic' heading's prose covers both positions (including the Elijah possibility) as part of explaining the natati lecha framework, while the current 'Possibility Argument' heading focuses only on Rabbi Eliezer's side — however, since the passage actually contains both sides of the dispute and the essay appears to have split them across two sections, the current placement under 'Possibility Argument' is defensible since that section's prose explicitly quotes the Elijah phrase that appears in this passage.

Both items together constitute the objection that Shmuel's ruling cannot refer to Rabbi Shimon of the mishna because that would be redundant — Shmuel already rules that davar she-eino mitkavein is permitted, as confirmed by Rav Ḥanin bar Ashi and Rav Ḥiyya bar Avin — which is precisely what candidate 2 ('If Mishna') describes.

The passage explicitly states the ruling must refer to Rabbi Shimon of the baraita and that Rav Sheisha explicitly transmits 'halacha ke-Rabbi Shimon de-baraita,' which is precisely what the 'Must Be Baraita' section's prose discusses.

The mishna introduces the case of slitting a firstborn's ear and presents both Rabbi Eliezer's and the Rabbis' positions together, matching heading 0's prose which describes the introductory mishna and notes that all agree shechita on the deliberately inflicted mum is never permissible — the subsequent headings discuss the Gemara's analysis of each opinion separately.

The passage opens with the Gemara's challenge 'does Rabbi Eliezer penalize forever?' and raises the tzaraat contradiction — this is exactly the 'Question Severity' section's content (prompting a challenge and sharpening it with a contrasting case), whereas candidate 3 'Tzaraat Parallel' describes the resolution/analysis of that case, which would follow after this challenge is introduced.
The passage is the direct quote of Rabbah and Rav Yosef's resolution distinguishing property from body penalties, which is exactly what the 'Rabbah Resolves' section's prose describes.

The passage explicitly articulates Rabbi Eliezer's deterrence-based reasoning — distinguishing property (where temptation is real and downside negligible) from body (where suffering already deters) — which is exactly what the 'Policy: Deterrent' section's prose describes.

All three items are Rava's challenge about the Rabbis' apparent contradiction between the two mishnayot and its resolution — exactly what the 'Rava Question' prose describes — not the policy/deterrent framework of the current placement under 'Policy: Deterrent'.
